claim: ROCK1 and ROCK2 are Rho-GTPase effectors that control key aspects of the actin cytoskeleton.
source: Rho-associated kinases 1 and 2 (ROCK1/2) are Rho-GTPase effectors that control key aspects of the actin cytoskeleton, but their role in proliferation and cancer initiation or progression is not known.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background information.

claim: ROCK1 and ROCK2 act redundantly to maintain actomyosin contractility and cell proliferation.
source: Here, we provide evidence that ROCK1 and ROCK2 act redundantly to maintain actomyosin contractility and cell proliferation and that their loss leads to cell-cycle arrest and cellular senescence.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Loss of ROCK1 and ROCK2 leads to cell-cycle arrest and cellular senescence.
source: Here, we provide evidence that ROCK1 and ROCK2 act redundantly to maintain actomyosin contractility and cell proliferation and that their loss leads to cell-cycle arrest and cellular senescence.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Loss of ROCK1 and ROCK2 causes down-regulation of CyclinA, CKS1 and CDK1.
source: This phenotype arises from down-regulation of the essential cell-cycle proteins CyclinA, CKS1 and CDK1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by western blot and mass spectrometry data in Figure 4.

claim: Loss of either Rock1 or Rock2 alone has no negative impact on tumorigenesis in mouse models of non-small cell lung cancer and melanoma.
source: Accordingly, while the loss of either Rock1 or Rock2 had no negative impact on tumorigenesis in mouse models of non-small cell lung cancer and melanoma, loss of both blocked tumor formation, as no tumors arise in which both Rock1 and Rock2 have been genetically deleted.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by tumor data in Figures 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of both Rock1 and Rock2 blocks tumor formation.
source: Accordingly, while the loss of either Rock1 or Rock2 had no negative impact on tumorigenesis in mouse models of non-small cell lung cancer and melanoma, loss of both blocked tumor formation, as no tumors arise in which both Rock1 and Rock2 have been genetically deleted.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by retention of ROCK protein in tumors shown in Figure 6.

claim: No tumors arise in which both Rock1 and Rock2 have been genetically deleted.
source: Accordingly, while the loss of either Rock1 or Rock2 had no negative impact on tumorigenesis in mouse models of non-small cell lung cancer and melanoma, loss of both blocked tumor formation, as no tumors arise in which both Rock1 and Rock2 have been genetically deleted.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by SRM and western blot data showing retention of ROCK protein in tumors in Figure 6.

claim: ROCK regulates cell cycle progression and tumorigenesis possibly through the maintenance of cellular contractility.
source: Our results reveal an indispensable role for ROCK, yet redundant role for isoforms 1 and 2, in cell cycle progression and tumorigenesis, possibly through the maintenance of cellular contractility.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings, with the word 'possibly' indicating some speculation.

claim: ROCK1 and ROCK2 are activated by interaction with Rho GTPases.
source: They are activated by interaction with Rho GTPases and act through a number of pathways to regulate the actin cytoskeleton and thus cell migration, cell-cell adhesion and cancer cell invasion (Itoh et al., 1999; Olson and Sahai, 2009; Thumkeo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ROCKs regulate the actin cytoskeleton and thus cell migration, cell-cell adhesion and cancer cell invasion.
source: They are activated by interaction with Rho GTPases and act through a number of pathways to regulate the actin cytoskeleton and thus cell migration, cell-cell adhesion and cancer cell invasion (Itoh et al., 1999; Olson and Sahai, 2009; Thumkeo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Substrates for ROCKs include MYPT1 and MLC, which regulate actomyosin contractile forces.
source: Substrates for ROCKs include the myosin-binding subunit of myosin phosphatase (MYPT1) and the myosin regulatory light chain (MLC), which regulate actomyosin contractile forces (Kawano et al., 1999; Kureishi et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Actomyosin contractility is generated when MLC is phosphorylated, allowing myosin II interaction with actin filaments to generate mechanical force.
source: Actomyosin contractility is generated when myosin regulatory light chain (MLC) is phosphorylated, allowing myosin II interaction with actin filaments to generate mechanical force (Aksoy et al., 1983; Kureishi et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ROCKs may directly phosphorylate MLC.
source: ROCKs may either directly phosphorylate MLC (Amano et al., 1996) or indirectly regulate MLC phosphorylation by phosphorylating the myosin-binding subunit of myosin phosphatase (MYPT1) and inactivating it (Kimura et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ROCKs indirectly regulate MLC phosphorylation by phosphorylating MYPT1 and inactivating it.
source: ROCKs may either directly phosphorylate MLC (Amano et al., 1996) or indirectly regulate MLC phosphorylation by phosphorylating the myosin-binding subunit of myosin phosphatase (MYPT1) and inactivating it (Kimura et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Myosin phosphatase inactivation results from phosphorylation of Thr696 and Thr850 on MYPT1.
source: Myosin phosphatase inactivation results from phosphorylation of two inhibitory sites, Thr696 and Thr850, on MYPT1 (Feng et al., 1999; Kawano et al., 1999; Muranyi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ROCKs phosphorylate and activate LIMK1 and LIMK2, which inhibit Cofilin.
source: Furthermore, ROCKs phosphorylate and activate LIM kinases 1 and 2 (LIMK1, 2), which inhibit the actin-depolymerizing protein Cofilin (Yang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ROCK1 and ROCK2 exhibit 65% overall identity and 87% identity within the kinase domain.
source: ROCK1 and 2 exhibit 65% overall identity and 87% within the kinase domain, and some studies suggest differential roles for the isoforms.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: ROCK1 is important for stress fiber formation in fibroblasts, whereas ROCK2 controls cortical contractility and phagocytosis.
source: Using RNA interference, ROCK1 was reported to be important for stress fiber formation in fibroblasts, whereas ROCK2 controls cortical contractility and phagocytosis (Yoneda et al., 2005; 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations from previous studies.

claim: Distinct roles for ROCK1 and ROCK2 have been described in the regulation of keratinocyte differentiation and cell detachment.
source: Distinct roles for ROCK1 and 2 have also been described in the regulation of keratinocyte differentiation (Lock and Hotchin, 2009) and cell detachment (Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations from previous studies.

claim: Rock1 knockout mice are born but have defects in eyelid and ventral body wall closure.
source: Mice in which Rock1 has been genetically deleted are born, but have defects in eyelid as well as ventral body wall closure (Shimizu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Ninety percent of Rock2 null mice die in utero due to defects in the placental labyrinth layer.
source: Ninety percent of Rock2 null mice die in utero due to defects in the placental labyrinth layer.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: ROCK1 cannot compensate for a loss of ROCK2 in placental development.
source: This indicates that ROCK1 cannot compensate for a loss of ROCK2.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from the Rock2 knockout phenotype.

claim: Rock2 null mice that are born display defects similar to those described in Rock1 null mice, indicating some level of functional redundancy.
source: However, the few Rock2 null mice, that are born, display defects similar to those described in Rock1 null mice (Thumkeo et al., 2003). This indicates some level of functional redundancy (Thumkeo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ROCKs have been reported to modulate apoptosis and cell proliferation.
source: In addition to their role in cell migration, ROCKs have been reported to modulate apoptosis (Coleman et al., 2001; Sebbagh et al., 2005) and cell proliferation (Croft and Olson, 2006; Samuel et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Some reports suggest ROCK function is required for G1/S progression.
source: The precise role of ROCKs in cell proliferation is not clear: some reports suggest ROCK function is required for G1/S progression (Croft and Olson, 2006; Zhang et al., 2009), but others suggest ROCK is only required for anchorage-independent growth of transformed cells (Sahai et al., 1999; Vigil et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations from previous studies.

claim: Some reports suggest ROCK is only required for anchorage-independent growth of transformed cells.
source: The precise role of ROCKs in cell proliferation is not clear: some reports suggest ROCK function is required for G1/S progression (Croft and Olson, 2006; Zhang et al., 2009), but others suggest ROCK is only required for anchorage-independent growth of transformed cells (Sahai et al., 1999; Vigil et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations from previous studies.

claim: Over-activation of ROCK by expressing the kinase domain of ROCK2 in mouse skin led to hyperproliferation and epidermal thickening.
source: One in vivo study reported that over-activation of ROCK, by expressing the kinase domain of ROCK2 in mouse skin, led to hyperproliferation and epidermal thickening (Samuel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Depletion of ROCK1 and ROCK2 resulted in a strong impairment of cell proliferation in vitro.
source: Depletion of ROCK1 and ROCK2 (Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆) resulted in a strong impairment of cell proliferation in vitro, which was not observed in cells lacking either ROCK1 (Rock1∆/∆) or ROCK2 (Rock2∆/∆) (Figure 1A), demonstrating that ROCK function is required for cell proliferation and that ROCK1 and ROCK2 act redundantly.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Cells lacking either ROCK1 or ROCK2 alone do not show impaired proliferation.
source: Depletion of ROCK1 and ROCK2 (Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆) resulted in a strong impairment of cell proliferation in vitro, which was not observed in cells lacking either ROCK1 (Rock1∆/∆) or ROCK2 (Rock2∆/∆) (Figure 1A), demonstrating that ROCK function is required for cell proliferation and that ROCK1 and ROCK2 act redundantly.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ROCK function is required for cell proliferation.
source: Depletion of ROCK1 and ROCK2 (Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆) resulted in a strong impairment of cell proliferation in vitro, which was not observed in cells lacking either ROCK1 (Rock1∆/∆) or ROCK2 (Rock2∆/∆) (Figure 1A), demonstrating that ROCK function is required for cell proliferation and that ROCK1 and ROCK2 act redundantly.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by proliferation data in Figure 1A.

claim: Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells eventually recover their ability to proliferate due to retention of ROCK1 and ROCK2 expression from uninfected cells.
source: Infection of cells with adenovirus is not 100% efficient, and when the growth of Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells was monitored over a longer period of time, these cells eventually recovered their ability to proliferate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), but western blot analysis revealed that these cells express ROCK1 and 2 in equivalent levels to wild type cells (data not shown) and thus likely originated from uninfected cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cells treated for 48 hr with the ROCK inhibitor H1152 had reduced proliferation.
source: Cells treated for 48 hr with the ROCK inhibitor H1152 (Sasaki et al., 2002) had reduced proliferation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: ROCK inhibitors GSK269962A, AT13148, GSK429286A and chroman1 cause reduced proliferation.
source: Similar results were observed with other ROCK inhibitors, such as GSK269962A, AT13148, GSK429286A and chroman1 (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: Y-27632 has a much weaker effect on cell proliferation than H1152.
source: However, the much-used ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 (Narumiya et al., 2000) had a much weaker effect on cell proliferation than H1152 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Y-27632 is a less effective ROCK inhibitor than H1152.
source: This is consistent with previous studies, where we have shown that Y-27632 is a less effective ROCK inhibitor than H1152 (Sadok et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Cells treated with blebbistatin for 48 hr displayed a similar proliferation defect to Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells.
source: To determine whether defects in proliferation were due to ROCK-mediated effects on actomyosin contractility, cells were treated with blebbistatin, an inhibitor of myosin II ATPase, for 48 hr. Treated cells displayed a similar proliferation defect to that observed in Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells (Figure 1B), arguing that the requirement for ROCK in cell proliferation is mediated through its role in maintaining actomyosin contractility.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: The requirement for ROCK in cell proliferation is mediated through its role in maintaining actomyosin contractility.
source: To determine whether defects in proliferation were due to ROCK-mediated effects on actomyosin contractility, cells were treated with blebbistatin, an inhibitor of myosin II ATPase, for 48 hr. Treated cells displayed a similar proliferation defect to that observed in Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells (Figure 1B), arguing that the requirement for ROCK in cell proliferation is mediated through its role in maintaining actomyosin contractility.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by blebbistatin treatment data in Figure 1B.

claim: Transformed Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ MEFs grew significantly slower in vivo compared to controls.
source: In contrast, transformed Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ MEFs grew significantly slower in vivo compared to controls (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by tumor growth data in Figure 1E.

claim: Tumors derived from Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ MEFs retained ROCK1 and ROCK2 protein.
source: Western Blot analysis revealed the retention of ROCK1 and 2 protein in tumors derived from Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ (Trp53 DD; H-RasV12) MEFs but complete deletion of ROCK1 in Rock1∆/∆ and ROCK2 in Rock2∆/∆ tumor samples (Figure 1F, data not shown), in agreement with the observed results on proliferation in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 1F.

claim: Injected Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells are unable to proliferate and form tumors.
source: This result shows that injected Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells are unable to proliferate and form tumors but the un-infected cells can proliferate and form tumors thereby accounting for the delay in tumorigenesis and implying that ROCK function is essential for proliferation and hence tumor initiation and formation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the tumor growth and western blot data.

claim: ROCK function is essential for proliferation and hence tumor initiation and formation.
source: This result shows that injected Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells are unable to proliferate and form tumors but the un-infected cells can proliferate and form tumors thereby accounting for the delay in tumorigenesis and implying that ROCK function is essential for proliferation and hence tumor initiation and formation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the tumor growth and western blot data.

claim: Three days after infection with Ad-Cre, Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells lacked stress fibers and displayed a 'tail retraction' phenotype.
source: Three days after infection with Ad-Cre, Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells lacked stress fibers and displayed a 'tail retraction' phenotype, a well-known characteristic of ROCK inhibition (Somlyo et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunofluorescence images in Figure 2A.

claim: Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells had long processes and defects in detaching their tails.
source: Cells had long processes and defects in detaching their tails, in contrast to their controls (Figure 2A and Videos 1,2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by images in Figure 2A and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: A similar tail retraction phenotype was observed in cells treated with H1152 or blebbistatin.
source: A similar phenotype was observed in cells treated with the ROCK inhibitor H1152 or the myosin II inhibitor blebbistatin but not in cells lacking either ROCK1 (Rock1∆/∆) or ROCK2 (Rock2∆/∆) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by images in Figure 2A.

claim: After five days, cells lacking both ROCK1 and ROCK2 had few apparent central stress fibers and adopted a flat morphology.
source: After five days, cells that lack both ROCK1 and ROCK2 had few apparent central stress fibers, unlike control cells, and surprisingly adopted a flat morphology (Figure 2A and Videos 1,2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by images in Figure 2A and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Migration speed and directionality were significantly increased in cells lacking ROCK1 and ROCK2 between Days 3 and 4 after adenovirus infection.
source: Interestingly, when random motility was analyzed between Days 3 and 4 after adenovirus infection, using ImageJ to track cells, migration speed and directionality were significantly increased in cells lacking ROCK1 and 2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Increased migration speed and directionality in Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells was previously described by Lomakin et al.
source: This was previously described by Lomakin et al. (Lomakin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Phosphorylation of MYPT and MLC were only affected in cells where both ROCKs had been removed.
source: Consistent with the levels of stress fibers, phosphorylation of MYPT and MLC were only affected in cells where both ROCKs had been removed (Figure 2B–C, quantification in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), showing that ROCK1 and ROCK2 act redundantly in regulating MYPT and MLC phosphorylation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 2B-C.

claim: ROCK1 and ROCK2 act redundantly in regulating MYPT and MLC phosphorylation.
source: Consistent with the levels of stress fibers, phosphorylation of MYPT and MLC were only affected in cells where both ROCKs had been removed (Figure 2B–C, quantification in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), showing that ROCK1 and ROCK2 act redundantly in regulating MYPT and MLC phosphorylation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 2B-C.

claim: MYPT Thr850 phosphorylation was markedly reduced in Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells.
source: While MYPT Thr850 phosphorylation was markedly reduced in Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells, MYPT Thr696 phosphorylation was not (Figure 2B, quantification in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that, while Thr850 is principally regulated by ROCKs, Thr696 is regulated by other kinases such as MRCK (Wilkinson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 2B.

claim: MYPT Thr696 phosphorylation was not reduced in Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells.
source: While MYPT Thr850 phosphorylation was markedly reduced in Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells, MYPT Thr696 phosphorylation was not (Figure 2B, quantification in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that, while Thr850 is principally regulated by ROCKs, Thr696 is regulated by other kinases such as MRCK (Wilkinson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 2B.

claim: Thr850 of MYPT is principally regulated by ROCKs, while Thr696 is regulated by other kinases such as MRCK.
source: While MYPT Thr850 phosphorylation was markedly reduced in Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells, MYPT Thr696 phosphorylation was not (Figure 2B, quantification in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that, while Thr850 is principally regulated by ROCKs, Thr696 is regulated by other kinases such as MRCK (Wilkinson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the western blot data, with a supporting citation.

claim: Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ MEFs spread when plated on a thick layer of collagen, indicating reduced cellular contractility.
source: Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ MEFs spread when plated on a thick layer of collagen 5 days after adenovirus infection, unlike Rock1∆/∆ or Rock2∆/∆ cells which had a more spindle-like morphology similar to wild-type controls (Figure 2D). This indicates reduced cellular contractility upon loss of ROCK1 and 2.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by images in Figure 2D.

claim: Cells lacking both ROCK1 and ROCK2 were unable to contract a collagen gel.
source: As a functional measure of actomyosin contractility, we used a gel contraction assay (Hooper et al., 2010), demonstrating that cells containing only ROCK1 or ROCK2 were able to contract a collagen gel, but cells lacking both ROCK1 and ROCK2 were not (Figure 2E), supporting the notion ROCK1 and ROCK2 act redundantly to maintain cellular contractility.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by gel contraction assay data in Figure 2E.

claim: ROCK1 and ROCK2 act redundantly to maintain cellular contractility.
source: As a functional measure of actomyosin contractility, we used a gel contraction assay (Hooper et al., 2010), demonstrating that cells containing only ROCK1 or ROCK2 were able to contract a collagen gel, but cells lacking both ROCK1 and ROCK2 were not (Figure 2E), supporting the notion ROCK1 and ROCK2 act redundantly to maintain cellular contractility.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by gel contraction assay data in Figure 2E.

claim: Short-term inhibition of ROCK using H1152 resulted in a significant decrease in phosphorylation of many phospho-sites, including Cofilin-1, Cofilin-2, Destrin, and MLC.
source: Short-term inhibition of ROCK, using H1152, resulted in a significant decrease in phosphorylation of many phospho-sites, including several known targets of ROCK such as Cofilin-1 (Ser-3), Cofilin-2 (Ser-3), Destrin (Ser-3), and Ser-19/Thr-20 of MLC (Supplementary file 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The majority of phosphorylation sites affected by short-term ROCK inhibition were fully recovered in long-term ROCK inhibited cells, with the exception of MLC Ser-19/Thr-20.
source: However, the majority of these phosphorylation sites, with the exception of MLC Ser-19/Thr-20, were only transiently affected, as their phosphorylation was fully recovered in long-term ROCK inhibited cells (Supplementary file 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) or Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by mass spectrometry and western blot data.

claim: No other kinase previously implicated in MLC phosphorylation can substitute for ROCK1/2 in the generation of actomyosin contractility.
source: These results indicate that alternative phosphorylation mechanisms exist for some ROCK substrates, but that no other kinase previously implicated in MLC phosphorylation can substitute for ROCK1/2 in the generation of actomyosin contractility.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the mass spectrometry and western blot data.

claim: Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ MEFs exhibited a significant increase in staining for senescence-associated β-galactosidase.
source: Indeed, Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ MEFs, or MEFs treated with H1152 or blebbistatin for prolonged periods exhibited a significant increase in staining for senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-βGal) (Debacq-Chainiaux et al., 2009) than control cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by SA-βGal staining data in Figure 3A.

claim: Senescence was observed after prolonged treatment with ROCK inhibitors GSK269962A, AT13148, GSK429286A and chroman1.
source: Senescence was also observed after prolonged treatment with other ROCK inhibitors such as GSK269962A, AT13148, GSK429286A and chroman1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment with AT13148 decreased tumor growth in 690cl2 melanoma cells injected into mice.
source: 690cl2 mouse melanoma cells were injected intra-dermally into CD1 athymic mice, and the mice treated with AT13148 at 40 mg/kg. Senescence was detected by SA-βGal staining of tumors. We observed a decrease in tumor growth when mice were treated with AT13148 compared to controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by tumor growth data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Treatment with AT13148 increased the number of SA-βGal positive cells within tumors.
source: Additionally, we observed an increase in the number of SA-βGal positive cells within tumors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by SA-βGal staining data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells showed a significant increase in the number of cells with two nuclei, indicating a failure of cytokinesis.
source: Analysis of Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells by microscopy revealed a significant increase in the number of cells with two nuclei (Figure 3B), indicating a failure of cytokinesis.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by microscopy data in Figure 3B.

claim: A greater percentage of Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells failed to divide compared to wild-type cells.
source: Analysis of time-lapse movies further confirmed a role for ROCK1 and 2 in cytokinesis as a greater percentage of Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells failed to divide compare to wild-type cells (Figure 3C and Videos 3,4).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by time-lapse data in Figure 3C and Videos 3 and 4.

claim: Analysis of time-lapse movies of Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells revealed an overall lower number of dividing cells.
source: In addition to an increased number of binucleate cells, analysis of time-lapse movies of Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells revealed an overall lower number of dividing cells (Figure 3D and Videos 3,4).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by time-lapse data in Figure 3D and Videos 3 and 4.

claim: Cells depleted of ROCK1 and ROCK2 do not initiate division, indicating a cell cycle block.
source: These data suggest that cells depleted of ROCK1 and 2 do not initiate division further, thus indicating a cell cycle block.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the time-lapse data.

claim: Fewer Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ MEFs were in G1 or S phase, and a higher percentage of cells were in G2/M phase of the cell cycle.
source: Fewer double knockout than wild-type MEFs were in G1 or S phase, and a higher percentage of cells in G2/M phase of the cell cycle (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3E.

claim: In Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells, distribution of cells in the three cell cycle phases is very similar between control treated and nocodazole treated cells.
source: In Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells, however, distribution of cells in the three cell cycle phases is very similar between control treated and nocodazole treated cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ROCK depletion causes a cell cycle block prior to G2/M, likely in the G1 phase of the cell cycle.
source: These data suggest that ROCK depletion causes a cell cycle block prior to G2/M. As there is an overall decrease in S phase cells, the block is likely to be in the G1 phase of the cell cycle.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the nocodazole treatment data.

claim: Inactivation of Trp53 and Rb did not prevent the senescence phenotype caused by loss of ROCK.
source: To determine whether blockade of Rb or Trp53 function would overcome senescence resulting from abrogation of ROCK function, we stably infected Rock1f/f;Rock2f/fMEFs with simian virus 40 large T-antigen (SV40 Large T), which is known to inactivate the tumor suppressors Trp53 and Rb (DeCaprio et al., 1988; Kierstead and Tevethia, 1993). The cells were then infected with Ad-Cre, to generate Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). Inactivation of Trp53 and Rb did not prevent the senescence phenotype caused by loss of ROCK, and cells displayed a similar growth defect to the one observed in Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ MEFs without SV40 Large T (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆;Trp53∆/∆ MEFs underwent senescence and were defective in their proliferation.
source: To further confirm that the senescent phenotype did not involve activation of Trp53, MEFs were isolated from Rock1f/f;Rock2f/f;Trp53f/f mice and ROCK and Trp53 depleted in vitro by Ad-Cre infection. Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆;Trp53∆/∆ MEFs were found to undergo senescence, and were defective in their proliferation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Treatment of Trp53 wild type and null cells with ROCK inhibitors H1152 and GSK269962A increased senescence compared to control cells.
source: We then treated Trp53 wild type and null cells with the ROCK inhibitors H1152 and GSK269962A and found an increase in senescence compared to control cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The classical senescence pathways did not seem to be affected in Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells or cells treated for prolonged periods with H1152.
source: Therefore, the classical senescence pathways did not seem to be affected in Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells or cells treated for prolonged periods with H1152.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the Trp53 and Rb inactivation experiments.

claim: Long-term ROCK inhibition revealed many cell cycle-related protein categories that were significantly modulated.
source: Annotation enrichment analysis (Cox and Mann, 2008) of the proteome-wide changes after long-term ROCK inhibition revealed many cell cycle-related protein categories that were significantly modulated in ROCK-inhibited cells (Supplementary file 2), consistent with a prominent cell-cycle phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by mass spectrometry data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: No significant changes were detected in the levels of known G1 cell-cycle arrest and senescence regulators such as p16, p19, p27, p21, CyclinD1, CyclinE, or phosphorylation of Rb.
source: However, when we analyzed proteins that are known to control G1 cell-cycle arrest and senescence, we did not detect significant changes in the levels of these proteins. These included known regulators, such as p16, p19, p27, p21, CyclinD1, CyclinE, or phosphorylation of Rb (Supplementary file 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by mass spectrometry and western blot data.

claim: CDK1, CyclinA and CKS1 protein levels were significantly reduced upon loss of and long-term inhibition of ROCK1 and ROCK2.
source: However, CDK1, CyclinA and CKS1 protein levels were significantly reduced upon loss of and long-term inhibition of ROCK1 and 2 (Supplementary file 2 and Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by mass spectrometry and western blot data in Figure 4A-C and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Long-term treatment of cells with active blebbistatin decreased the levels of CDK1, CyclinA and CKS1.
source: Long-term treatment of cells with blebbistatin (blebbistatin +/-), but not the inactive enantiomer (blebbistatin +), also decreased the levels of CDK1, CyclinA and CKS1 (Figure 4B,C), suggesting that it is loss of contractility downstream of ROCK loss that results in down-regulation of these proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Loss of contractility downstream of ROCK loss results in down-regulation of CDK1, CyclinA and CKS1.
source: Long-term treatment of cells with blebbistatin (blebbistatin +/-), but not the inactive enantiomer (blebbistatin +), also decreased the levels of CDK1, CyclinA and CKS1 (Figure 4B,C), suggesting that it is loss of contractility downstream of ROCK loss that results in down-regulation of these proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the blebbistatin treatment data.

claim: In Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells, Cdk1 and Ccna2 mRNA levels were significantly reduced, whereas Cks1b mRNA remained unchanged.
source: Analysis of mRNA levels revealed that, in Rock1∆/∆/Rock2∆/∆ cells, Cdk1 and Ccna2 mRNA levels were significantly reduced, whereas Cks1b mRNA remained unchanged (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by qPCR data in Figure 4D.

claim: Cells depleted of CKS1, CDK1 or CyclinA were unable to proliferate.
source: Cells depleted of CKS1, CDK1 or CyclinA were unable to proliferate (Figure 5A) and had increased staining for SA-βGal (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by colony formation data in Figure 5A.

claim: Cells depleted of CKS1, CDK1 or CyclinA had increased staining for SA-βGal.
source: Cells depleted of CKS1, CDK1 or CyclinA were unable to proliferate (Figure 5A) and had increased staining for SA-βGal (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by SA-βGal staining data in Figure 5B.

claim: Knockdown of Cks1b affected protein levels of CDK1 and CyclinA.
source: We found that knockdown of Cks1b affected protein levels of CDK1 and CyclinA, while knockdown of Cdk1 affected protein levels of CKS1 and CyclinA and knockdown of Ccna2 affected levels of CKS1 and CDK1 (Figure 5C), confirming a clear link between the expression of these proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 5C.

claim: Knockdown of Cdk1 affected protein levels of CKS1 and CyclinA.
source: We found that knockdown of Cks1b affected protein levels of CDK1 and CyclinA, while knockdown of Cdk1 affected protein levels of CKS1 and CyclinA and knockdown of Ccna2 affected levels of CKS1 and CDK1 (Figure 5C), confirming a clear link between the expression of these proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 5C.

claim: Knockdown of Ccna2 affected levels of CKS1 and CDK1.
source: We found that knockdown of Cks1b affected protein levels of CDK1 and CyclinA, while knockdown of Cdk1 affected protein levels of CKS1 and CyclinA and knockdown of Ccna2 affected levels of CKS1 and CDK1 (Figure 5C), confirming a clear link between the expression of these proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 5C.

claim: Cell cycle proteins CKS1, CDK1 and CyclinA are downregulated upon loss of actomyosin contractility.
source: Overall, these results indicate that cell cycle proteins CKS1, CDK1 and CyclinA are downregulated upon loss of actomyosin contractility, and their depletion causes defects in cell proliferation and increased cellular senescence.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Depletion of CKS1, CDK1 and CyclinA causes defects in cell proliferation and increased cellular senescence.
source: Overall, these results indicate that cell cycle proteins CKS1, CDK1 and CyclinA are downregulated upon loss of actomyosin contractility, and their depletion causes defects in cell proliferation and increased cellular senescence.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: The total tumor area was increased in Rock1f/f mice in the NSCLC model.
source: Histological analysis revealed that the total tumor area was increased in Rock1f/f mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by histological data in Figure 6A.

claim: ROCK1 may have a tumor suppressor function in the NSCLC mouse model.
source: This result suggests that ROCK1 may have a tumor suppressor function in this specific mouse model, of which the mechanism requires further investigation and will be the subject of another manuscript.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the tumor area data, with speculation about future work.

claim: No difference was seen comparing tumor area of Rock1f/f;Rock2f/f or Rock2f/f with wild type mice in the NSCLC model.
source: However, no difference was seen comparing tumor area of Rock1f/f;Rock2f/f or Rock2f/f with wild type mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by histological data in Figure 6A.

claim: Cell lines generated from Rock1f/f;Rock2f/f;KrasG12D;Trp53R270H-driven tumors always retained ROCK1 or ROCK2 protein.
source: Western blot analysis of cell lines generated from Rock1f/f;Rock2f/f;KrasG12D; Trp53R270H-driven tumors showed that they always retained ROCK1 or ROCK2 protein (Figure 6B) and contained un-recombined floxed alleles of Rock1 and 2.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data in Figure 6B.

claim: Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells failed to proliferate when compared to control cells in a colony formation assay.
source: Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells, but not Rock1∆/wt;Rock2∆/∆ cells, failed to proliferate when compared to the control cells in a colony formation assay (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by colony formation data in Figure 6C.

claim: One wild-type allele of Rock is sufficient to allow cell proliferation.
source: This further highlights the fact that one wild-type allele of Rock is sufficient to allow cell proliferation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the colony formation data in Figure 6C.

claim: In cell lines derived from tumors in Rock1f/f;Rock2f/f mice, either ROCK1 or ROCK2 protein was always retained.
source: SRM analysis showed that, in cell lines derived from tumors in Rock1f/f;Rock2f/fmice, either ROCK1 or ROCK2 protein was always retained (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by SRM data in Figure 6D.

claim: ROCK1 and ROCK2 protein was absent in cell lines derived from Rock1f/f or Rock2f/f tumor bearing mice, respectively.
source: ROCK1 and ROCK2 protein was absent in cell lines derived from Rock1f/f or Rock2f/ftumor bearing mice, respectively (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by SRM data in Figure 6D.

claim: ROCK1 protein was not up-regulated in cell lines or tumors from mice with Rock2f/f genotype in a compensatory manner and vice versa.
source: Importantly, ROCK1 protein was not up-regulated in cell lines or tumors from mice with Rock2f/f genotype in a compensatory manner and vice versa.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by SRM data in Figure 6D.

claim: The overall concentration of ROCK1 and ROCK2 proteins was found to be similar.
source: The overall concentration of ROCK1 and 2 proteins was found to be similar, excluding potential effects driven by differential isoform expression.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by SRM data in Figure 6D.

claim: No differences were found in onset of tumorigenesis when comparing BrafV600E with BrafV600E;Rock1f/f or BrafV600E;Rock1f/f;Rock2f/f mice in the melanoma model.
source: No differences were found in onset of tumorigenesis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) or survival (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) when comparing BrafV600E with BrafV600E;Rock1f/f or BrafV600E;Rock1f/f;Rock2f/f mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Tumor latency was decreased in BrafV600E;Rock2f/f mice.
source: Tumor latency was decreased in BrafV600E;Rock2f/fmice only but not in combination with Ptenf/f or Ptenf/wt (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Survival was decreased in BrafV600E;Rock2f/f mice as well as in combination with Ptenf/f.
source: Survival was also found to be decreased in BrafV600E:Rock2f/fmice as well as in combination with Ptenf/f (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that unlike in the NSCLC model, ROCK2 may be having a tumor suppressor role in this model.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ROCK2 may have a tumor suppressor role in the melanoma model.
source: Survival was also found to be decreased in BrafV600E:Rock2f/fmice as well as in combination with Ptenf/f (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that unlike in the NSCLC model, ROCK2 may be having a tumor suppressor role in this model.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the survival data.

claim: Analysis of cell lines generated from melanomas revealed retention of either ROCK protein in mice with Rock1f/f;Rock2f/f genotype.
source: Nevertheless, similar to the NSCLC model, analysis of cell lines generated from these melanomas, by SRM and immunoblotting, revealed retention of either ROCK protein in mice with Rock1f/f;Rock2f/fgenotype, but efficient excision of the floxed locus in mice with Rock1f/f and Rock2f/f genotypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by SRM and western blot data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: ROCK protein is required for tumorigenesis, since retention of at least one Rock allele is selected for in both Ras-driven lung tumors and Raf-driven melanomas.
source: These results further support our observation that ROCK protein is required for tumorigenesis, since retention of at least one Rock allele is selected for in both Ras-driven lung tumors and Raf-driven melanomas.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the tumor and cell line data.

claim: Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ melanoma cells failed to proliferate compared to control cells in a colony formation assay.
source: Furthermore, treatment of melanoma cell lines with Ad-Cre-GFP, to excise the retained Rock locus, revealed that Rock1∆/∆;Rock2∆/∆ cells but not Rock2∆/∆ cells fail to proliferate compared to control cells in a colony formation assay (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by colony formation data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The absence of ROCK1 and ROCK2 is incompatible with tumorigenesis.
source: Collectively, analysis of ROCK1 and ROCK2 protein expression in tumors and tumor derived cell lines suggests that the absence of ROCK1 and ROCK2 is incompatible with tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the tumor and cell line data.

claim: Either ROCK1 or ROCK2 protein is sufficient to promote tumorigenesis.
source: However, either ROCK1 or ROCK2 protein is sufficient to promote tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the tumor and cell line data.

claim: Either ROCK1 or ROCK2 is sufficient to regulate MLC and MYPT phosphorylation and thus actomyosin contractility.
source: Our data with genetic deletion in an isogenic fashion show that either ROCK1 or ROCK2 is sufficient to regulate MLC and MYPT phosphorylation and thus actomyosin contractility.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Cofilin phosphorylation is affected after short-term ROCK inhibition but recovers upon long-term treatment.
source: However, using quantitative mass spectrometry treatment of cells with the ROCK inhibitor H1152, we show that Cofilin phosphorylation is affected after short-term ROCK inhibition but recovers upon long-term treatment.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: Other kinases are able to take over and phosphorylate Cofilin upon long-term ROCK inhibition.
source: This indicates that other kinases are able to take over and phosphorylate Cofilin.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from the mass spectrometry data.

claim: ROCK is the major kinase regulating MLC phosphorylation.
source: MLC phosphorylation, however, is not recovered indicating that ROCK is the major kinase regulating MLC phosphorylation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from the mass spectrometry data.

claim: The depletion of ROCK1 and ROCK2 leads to severe defects in cell proliferation, which is not observed in cells lacking either ROCK1 or ROCK2.
source: We demonstrate that the depletion of ROCK1 and 2 leads to severe defects in cell proliferation, which is not observed in cells lacking either ROCK1 or 2.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Defects in cell proliferation are also observed in cells treated long-term with ROCK inhibitors or the MyosinII inhibitor blebbistatin.
source: Defects in cell proliferation are also observed in cells treated long-term with ROCK inhibitors or the MyosinII inhibitor blebbistatin.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Treatment with several ROCK inhibitors (H1152, GSK269962A, AT13148, GSK429286A and chroman1) could mimic the effects of genetic deletion of Rock1 and Rock2.
source: We believe that this may reflect the relatively low potency of Y-27632 as a ROCK inhibitor, since we found that treatment with several other ROCK inhibitors (H1152, GSK269962A, AT13148, GSK429286A and chroman1), which have been shown to be more potent than Y-27632 (Sadok et al., 2015), could mimic the effects of genetic deletion of Rock1 and Rock2.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: Cell proliferation defects upon deletion of ROCK1 and ROCK2 are due to a G1 arrest and a block in cytokinesis.
source: Cell proliferation defects upon deletion of ROCK1 and 2 are due to a G1 arrest and a block in cytokinesis.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The cell proliferation defects arising from abrogation of ROCK function result in cellular senescence, both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Interestingly, the cell proliferation defects arising from abrogation of ROCK function result in cellular senescence, both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Cellular senescence from ROCK loss does not appear to involve changes in levels of p16, p21, p27, but the down-regulation of CDK1, Cyclin A and CKS1.
source: This cellular senescence does not appear to involve changes in levels of the cell cycle inhibitors p16, p21, p27, but the down-regulation of cell-cycle proteins CDK1, Cyclin A and the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor CKS1.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: CKS1 is known to regulate levels of CDK1 and Cyclin A.
source: CKS1 is known to regulate levels of CDK1 and Cyclin A (Martinsson-Ahlzen et al., 2008; Westbrook et al., 2007), and can function in G1 and G2 phases of the cell cycle (Tang and Reed, 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Cks1b-/- cells are defective in proliferation, have reduced proportions of cells in S- and G1-phase, accumulation of cells with G2/M DNA content and exhibit senescence.
source: Interestingly, it has been shown that Cks1b-/- cells are defective in proliferation, have reduced proportions of cells in S- and G1-phase, accumulation of cells with G2/M DNA content (Hoellein et al., 2012; Spruck et al., 2001) and exhibit senescence.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: An essential function of ROCK in cell proliferation is to regulate the expression of CKS1.
source: We therefore propose that an essential function of ROCK in cell proliferation is to regulate the expression of CKS1.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: ROCK-driven CKS1 down-regulation is a novel marker of senescence.
source: In addition, this ROCK-driven CKS1 down-regulation is a novel marker of senescence.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: Treatment with blebbistatin led to cell cycle arrest, senescence and reduced levels of CKS1, CyclinA and CDK1.
source: We observed that treatment with blebbistatin a direct inhibitor of myosin II led to cell cycle arrest, senescence and reduced levels of CKS1, CyclinA and CDK1, potentially suggesting that ROCK-dependent regulation of cell proliferation is through the inhibition of actomyosin contractility rather than another target of ROCK signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: ROCK-dependent regulation of cell proliferation is potentially through the inhibition of actomyosin contractility rather than another target of ROCK signaling.
source: We observed that treatment with blebbistatin a direct inhibitor of myosin II led to cell cycle arrest, senescence and reduced levels of CKS1, CyclinA and CDK1, potentially suggesting that ROCK-dependent regulation of cell proliferation is through the inhibition of actomyosin contractility rather than another target of ROCK signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from the blebbistatin data, with the word 'potentially' indicating some speculation.

claim: Tumor formation is incompatible with homozygous deletion of both Rock1 and Rock2.
source: Using tumor samples as well as tumor derived cell lines, from two different genetically engineered mouse models of tumorigenesis, we find that tumor formation is incompatible with homozygous deletion of both Rock1 and Rock2, since tumors arising in Rock1f/f;Rock2f/f mice always retained either un-recombined Rock1f/for Rock2f/f alleles and showed expression of either ROCK1 or ROCK2, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the tumor data.

claim: Tumors arising in Rock1f/f;Rock2f/f mice always retained either un-recombined Rock1f/f or Rock2f/f alleles and showed expression of either ROCK1 or ROCK2.
source: Using tumor samples as well as tumor derived cell lines, from two different genetically engineered mouse models of tumorigenesis, we find that tumor formation is incompatible with homozygous deletion of both Rock1 and Rock2, since tumors arising in Rock1f/f;Rock2f/f mice always retained either un-recombined Rock1f/for Rock2f/f alleles and showed expression of either ROCK1 or ROCK2, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by tumor data in Figures 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of Rock1 appears to increase tumor burden in the NSCLC model.
source: Targeting either Rock1 or Rock2 appears to have mild and divergent consequences in the mouse models. Deletion of Rock1 appears to increase tumor burden in the NSCLC model, whereas deletion of Rock2 leads to decreased tumor onset and survival in the melanoma model.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by tumor data in Figure 6A.

claim: Deletion of Rock2 leads to decreased tumor onset and survival in the melanoma model.
source: Targeting either Rock1 or Rock2 appears to have mild and divergent consequences in the mouse models. Deletion of Rock1 appears to increase tumor burden in the NSCLC model, whereas deletion of Rock2 leads to decreased tumor onset and survival in the melanoma model.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by tumor data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The putative tumor suppressor functions of Rock1 and Rock2 do not appear to be a consequence of differential expression as the absolute concentration of the two isoforms was found to be similar by SRM.
source: These putative tumor suppressor functions of Rock1 and Rock2 do not appear to be a consequence of differential expression as the absolute concentration of the two isoforms was found to be similar by SRM.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by SRM data in Figure 6D.

claim: The retention of ROCK protein in Rock1f/f;Rock2f/f mice demonstrates that ROCK function is essential for tumorigenesis.
source: The retention of ROCK protein in Rock1f/f;Rock2f/f mice, however, demonstrates that ROCK function is essential for tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the tumor data.

claim: The activation of Cre recombinase leads to the formation of a mixed population of cells in which either Rock, or both Rock1 and 2, have been excised.
source: In the tumor models used in this study, excision of Rock alleles and tumor initiation are achieved simultaneously in an inducible fashion; therefore we propose that the activation of Cre recombinase leads to the formation of a mixed population of cells in which either Rock, or both Rock1 and 2, have been excised.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an explanation for the tumor data.

claim: ROCK1 and ROCK2 double-null cells are unable to form a tumor as they are defective in cell proliferation and senesce.
source: The ROCK1 and 2 double-null cells, however, are unable to form a tumor as they are defective in cell proliferation and senesce.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an explanation for the tumor data.

claim: Cells that have retained either Rock allele form tumors but these are the genetic equivalent of a single knockout.
source: The remaining cells, that is those that have retained either Rock allele form tumors but these are the genetic equivalent of a single knockout.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an explanation for the tumor data.

claim: Recent studies have identified a role for ROCK inhibition in combinatorial treatments in BRAF-mutant melanoma and Kras-driven lung cancers.
source: Recent studies have identified a role for ROCK inhibition in combinatorial treatments in BRAF-mutant melanoma (Smit et al., 2014), as well as in Kras-driven lung cancers (Kumar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The data provide a molecular basis for exploiting the use of effective ROCK inhibitors as anti-cancer agents either alone or in combination.
source: Our data thus provide a molecular basis, and highlight the need, for exploiting the use of effective ROCK inhibitors as anti-cancer agents either alone or in combination.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: Incomplete or specific inhibition of only one isoform of ROCK alone may not be an effective treatment, and may even lead to adverse results.
source: However, incomplete or specific inhibition of only one isoform of ROCK alone may not be an effective treatment, and may even lead to adverse results as our results also highlight isoform specific tumor suppressive functions for ROCK1 in lung and ROCK2 in melanoma models.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the experimental findings, with speculation about treatment implications.
